latin.437: Infanti in utero materno putasne ea peccata imputari, quae si vixisset, & ad senium pervenisset toto vitae tempore facturus fuisset? non arbitror. Cur igitur ei vis imputari peccatum actuale tunc admissum cum nondum erat, immo aliquot annorum millibus antequam esset, quodque adeo ipse nec actu, nec potentia commisit; non actu, quia non erat; non potentia, quia cum committeretur, non poterat tunc esse, hoc volo, non poterat esse respectu illius temporis quo peccatum illud perpetratum est, usque adeo ut implicet contradictionem illud idem numero quod vis nobis imputari a nobis fieri, aut factum esse. Nunquam illud fecimus, nec facere potuimus, nec ex quo nati sumus facere possumus.
latin.438: Praeclare author Hypognosticon Contra Pelagianos, sive is sit Augustinus, sive alius: Deus, inquit, praescius operum eius malorum, quae facturus erat aetate perfecta, periturum dixit de populo suo. Itane, Pelagiane insane, Deus qui justus est in omnibus viis suis & sanctus in omnibus operibus suis, pro huiusmodi credendus incircumcisum puerulum judicare, ut tanquam factorem pro non factis sceleribus puniat, tempus imputet quoddam ubi vita non vixerit, ubi velle & nolle non fuit voluntatis? Absit hoc apud judicem justum &c. Vide quantopere pius vir ab ista cogitatione abhorreat, Deum puerulo tempus imputare quoddam ubi vita non vixerit, quamvis potuerit vivere; quantumque id existimet non convenire Dei justitiae.
latin.439: Quid ergo diceret de eo tempore quum puerulus non modo vita non vivebat, sed ne poterat quidem vivere; deque peccato quod non modo non fecit, sed neque potuit unquam facere? Quod si Apostoli exemplo in Epistolis ad Gal. & ad Heb. velimus Scripturae verba & silentium accurate perpendere, quid est quamobrem non observemus in Interdicto, in sententia post violatum interdictum Adamo pronunciata nullam esse posteritatis factam mentionem? Cavit nimirum Deus jam tum, ne vobis ullam praeberet ansam ita de justitia sua, ut facitis, sentiendi.
latin.440: Sed fac interdictum illud nos ad obedientiam obligasse pro eo tempore quo nondum eramus, quo solus erat cum uxore in paradiso Adamus, quid a nobis requirebat? Ut ne ederemus de fructu arboris scientiae boni & mali? Paruimus: nam qui edere tum temporis non poteramus, profecto non edimus. Edimus, inquies, in Adamo. Bene habet: non igitur edimus in nobis. Quandoquidem igitur in uno Adamo manducavimus illum fructum, decuit nos etiam puniri in uno Adamo: ac cum in nostris personis non manducaverimus, non oportuit nos puniri in nostris personis.
latin.441: Scire velim quomodo ad nos interdictum spectabat, utrum quatenus sumus personae distinctae a persona Adami, an duntaxat quatenus nihil aliud eramus quam ipse Adamus? nostri enim tunc certe pars nulla erat, immo ne semen quidem unde procreati sumus, immo ne semen quidem ex quo centesimus a nobis parens noster ortus est. Prius non dixeris. Posterius si affirmas, quid est quamobrem ad nos non spectaverit interdictum, illius temporis respectu, nisi quatenus eramus nihil nisi ipse Adamus, velis autem comminationem adjunctam interdicto ad nos spectare quatenus personae sumus ab Adamo diversae & separatae? Equidem non intelligo cur ad nos alio modo interdictum, alio comminatio pertineat.
latin.442: Verum tu argumentaris ab eventu. Hoc enim violato interdicto & Adam & omnes posteri morti obnoxii facti sunt. Certe, sed Adam immediate ob violatum a se interdictum, posteri ob vitium & peccatum quod singulis ab Adamo propagatum inhaeret.

pass_a.437: Do you think sins an infant in the womb would have done if it had lived to old age are imputed to it? Placeus thinks not. Why then impute to it an actual sin committed when it did not yet exist—indeed thousands of years before—which it committed neither in act nor in potency: not in act because it was not; not in potency because when the sin was done it could not then be, with respect to that time—so far that it implies a contradiction that the very same numbered deed you want imputed to us was done by us. We never did it, could not do it, and since birth still cannot do it.
pass_a.438: Hypognosticon Against the Pelagians (Augustine or another) puts it well: God, knowing beforehand the evils one would do at full age, declared that one of his people would perish. Must the just and holy God therefore be thought to try an uncircumcised toddler as a doer, chastise undone crimes, and charge a span of life never lived—where willing and refusing were not yet of the will? Away with that before a just judge. Mark how the pious writer recoils from charging a child with unlived time, even if life was possible, and how alien he counts that to divine justice.
pass_a.439: Still more: what of a span when the child not only lacked life but could not live at all, and a deed it neither did nor ever could do? Following the Apostle's habit in Galatians and Hebrews of weighing both what Scripture says and what it withholds, why miss that the Interdict and the post-fall sentence on Adam name no posterity? God already then left you no foothold for reading his justice your way.
pass_a.440: Grant for argument that the ban obligated us while we still were not, Adam alone in paradise with his wife: its demand was simply not to eat that fruit. We kept it—those unable then to eat did not eat. If the reply is that we ate in Adam, then precisely we did not eat in ourselves. Eating in the one Adam fits punishment in the one Adam; not having eaten in our persons, we ought not be punished in our persons.
pass_a.441: Placeus wants to know how the interdict looked to us—as persons distinct from Adam's person, or only insofar as we were nothing but Adam himself? Then certainly no part of us existed, not even the seed from which we were begotten, not even the seed from which our hundredth parent sprang. You will not say the former. If you affirm the latter, why should the interdict, for that time, look to us only insofar as we were nothing but Adam, yet you want the threat joined to the interdict to look to us as persons diverse and separate from Adam? Placeus does not understand why the interdict should pertain one way and the threat another.
pass_a.442: But you argue from the event: when the ban was broken, Adam and all posterity were made liable to death. Certainly—but Adam immediately for the ban he himself violated; posterity for the vice and sin that, propagated from Adam, inheres in each. Tip before the sentence/common-penalty syllogism.

437: Do you think those sins are imputed to an infant in the mother's womb which, if it had lived and reached old age, it would have done through the whole time of life? I do not think so. Why then do you want an actual sin imputed to it that was then committed when it did not yet exist—indeed some thousands of years before it was—and which it itself committed neither in act nor in potency: not in act, because it was not; not in potency, because when it was being committed it could not then be—this is what I mean: it could not be with respect to that time in which that sin was perpetrated—so far that it implies a contradiction that that same numbered deed which you want imputed to us was done by us, or was done. We never did it, nor could we do it, nor since we were born can we do it.
438: Finely the author of the Hypognosticon Against the Pelagians—whether he is Augustine or another: God, he says, foreknowing its evil works which it was going to do in perfect age, said of his people that it would perish. Is it so, mad Pelagian—is God who is just in all his ways and holy in all his works to be believed, for such a reason, to judge an uncircumcised little child so as to punish him as a doer for crimes not done, to impute some time where life was not lived, where willing and nilling were not of the will? Far be this before a just judge, and so on. See how greatly the pious man abhors that thought—that God imputes to a little child some time where life was not lived, although it could have lived—and how much he judges that not to agree with God's justice.
439: What then would he say of that time when the little child not only was not living life, but could not even live; and of a sin which it not only did not do, but never could do? But if by the Apostle's example in the Epistles to the Galatians and to the Hebrews we wish carefully to weigh Scripture's words and silence, what reason is there why we should not observe that in the Interdict, in the sentence pronounced to Adam after the interdict was violated, no mention of posterity was made? God already then took care, to be sure, lest he should offer you any handle for sensing concerning his justice as you do.
440: But grant that that interdict bound us to obedience for that time when we did not yet exist, when Adam alone was in paradise with his wife—what did it require of us? That we should not eat of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? We obeyed: for those who at that time could not eat certainly did not eat. We ate, you will say, in Adam. Well and good: therefore we did not eat in ourselves. Since therefore in one Adam we ate that fruit, it was fitting that we also be punished in one Adam: and since we did not eat in our own persons, we ought not to have been punished in our own persons.
441: I should like to know how the interdict looked to us—whether insofar as we are persons distinct from Adam's person, or only insofar as we were nothing other than Adam himself? For then certainly no part of us existed, indeed not even the seed from which we were begotten, indeed not even the seed from which our hundredth parent sprang. You will not say the former. If you affirm the latter, what reason is there why the interdict should not have looked to us, with respect to that time, except insofar as we were nothing but Adam himself—yet you want the threat joined to the interdict to look to us insofar as we are persons diverse and separate from Adam? For my part I do not understand why the interdict should pertain to us in one way, the threat in another.
442: But you argue from the event. For this—when the interdict was violated, both Adam and all posterity were made liable to death. Certainly: but Adam immediately for the interdict violated by himself, posterity for the vice and sin which, propagated from Adam, inheres in each.
